utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, on behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber would like to greet everyone in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and all the staff present in the courtroom. As I have indicated, I indicated yesterday, we have deliberated on the request of the Defence for the delay in -- or time extension for the list of witnesses. On the 11th of November they asked for the date of the delivery of this list would be the 3rd of December. The Chamber has considered this request and authorises the Defence to produce this list on the 3rd of December, 2004, according to their submission. As far as the admission of exhibits is concerned, is the Prosecution in the position to give us their final position or would you like to do it some other day?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can do it now or we can do it after this witness if you so please. There are just about 13 exhibits that the Prosecution is objecting to on grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. You're saying that there are 13 documents. Can you give us a list of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Numbers 1197, which is number 4 on the list. Defence 1197; number 10 on the list, Defence document 1220; number 11 on the list, Defence document 1221, 1-2-2-1; number 12 on the list, Defence document 1225; number 13 on the list, Defence document 1233; number 14 on the list, Defence document 1234, 1234; number 17 on the list, Defence document 1240, 1240; number 21 on the list, Defence document 1249, 1249; number 23 on the list, Defence document 1253, 1253; number 24 on the list, Defence document 1254, 1254; number 25 on the list, Defence document 1256, 1256; number 28, Defence document 1271, 1271; and number 34, Defence document 1306. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution object to these documents as stated before, the grounds of relevance. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you well, you are objecting to numbers 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17, 21, 23, 24, 25, 28, and 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The first two documents are incorrect. It's numbers 3 and 4, not 7 and 9 on the list. 3 and 4. 1196 and 1197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Documents 3, 1196, and 4, 1197. Number 10, 11 and so on. You're saying that there -- that you're objecting on the grounds of relevance. Would the Defence like to reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I apologise. I'm going to look at every single document. I've just had an opportunity to look at documents number 3 and 4. Unlike my learned friend, I believe that these documents are relevant because these documents indicate that the municipal staff of the civilian protection had the authority to dispose with the abandoned houses, the houses abandoned by either Croats or some other population, that they had the authority to take things from those houses and provide the population with those things in order to protect their fields. The document also shows what efforts were made, given the fact that women's platoons had been established in order to protect crops and livestock in this area. In general terms, I would like to say that these two documents clearly show and display the authorities that different bodies had when it came to disposing with the things that existed in the abandoned houses. The witness recognised this document. I would like to say something about other documents in general terms. The Prosecution has offered this Trial Chamber a number of documents that have nothing to do with the counts of the indictment. The Prosecution has stated that these are circumstantial evidence and that through their qualification they will try and create a certain picture. From the very beginning, unlike the Prosecution, we have tried to show the Trial Chamber the actual authority that the army units had, that the civilian bodies had at the time. And we also tried to portray the events and measures that were taken, both by the military authorities as well as the civilian authorities in the area. The previous two exhibits have a direct link with the position of the Defence on the authorities that existed at the time and on the right to dispose with the property at the time. And that's why we believe these documents are relevant. The next document that the Prosecution believes is not relevant is the document which also is relative to the same issue, and their arguments are the same. It speaks of the obligations and responsibilities of the civilian protection in the protection of things in the houses abandoned by the Croatian population and giving these houses for safeguarding to civilian population and other population in the area. Document number 11 is an integral part of a bigger document which the document number is 20 and 21 which speaks of the measures that civilian protection took when it had found out that some of the property had been stolen for various houses, although the property had been intended for the refugees and displaced persons. So this document is an integral part of the investigation and the facts that were obtained with regard to this procedure. Document number 12 is very relevant because it points to the situation that existed in the area. We heard about this situation from a number of witnesses. This is a document that originates from the civilian protection. The witness recognised it as something that he saw already, but this document points to a number of problems and to a number of exhibits that we already had before this Trial Chamber. In this document number 1225, in its paragraph number 3, line 1, one can see -- read a clear answer to the question that you, Your Honours, have put to the witnesses. Despite the curfew and the ban of movement of civilians in the area, a number of civilians were observed taking away property from the abandoned houses. So every line in this document points to the crimes and the perpetrators who were not known at the time. This is, therefore, a very relevant document, a document that has a bearing on a number of counts in the indictment. Under number 13, document speaks of the measures which were taken in order to protect the civilian property. The civilian protection authorised one of the members of the civilian protection to protect his own property but also the property in the neighbouring buildings. This was done in view of the personnel and the equipment that they had at their disposal at the time. As the witness has explained to us, this person was one of the members of the civilian protection who patrolled terrain. Number 14 speaks about the movement and accommodation of refugees Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond in the area. This says that a lot of efforts were made in order to accommodate refugees in an organised way. This also served to protect people's property, to prevent looting and destruction. Bear in mind that the property was abandoned and it was physically impossible to protect it. Under number 17 on this list is our exhibit 1240 which also speaks of the ways refugees entered these buildings. You've heard from a number of witnesses and we believe that this is very relevant with regard to every count that speaks of looting and destruction of property. This document is very important. It was also drafted by the civilian protection. Under number 21, we have a document to which you, Your Honours, drew the witness's attention. On the one hand it speaks of the measures which were taken if it was found out that somebody had stolen property, and on the other hand it points to the relationship and attitude towards the people who were accommodated in the primary school. The relevance of this document is absolutely certain. Under number 23, the exhibit also speaks about the authorities that the civilian protection assigned to certain persons in order to empower them to protect certain houses in the village, and this is one of a number of measures that were taken at the time in order to protect the civilian property -- the property of the civilians who had abandoned the area. Under number 24, we go back to the same issue, the issue being the attitude of the civilian protection towards the property of the civilians. The civilian protection tried to put in place measures in order to feed the population that had remained in the area and thus prevent looting and the rampage of persons who moved around through the area. The witness mentioned a number of 100.000 -- or rather, 160.000 refugees who passed through the area. And the witness also spoke about the measures which were put in place by the civilian bodies and other organs in order to work on the land and provide for the -- provide food for the refugees and ultimately to prevent the population from resorting to the ultimate means, and that was theft. Under number 25, the exhibit is of the ultimate importance because it speaks of all the measures and all the problems and difficulties in the work of the civilian body of authority, whose task was to protect property that existed in the area. This document also speaks about the circumstances under which this body had to perform its tasks. At the same time, from the point of Defence, this document is of the utmost relevance because it shows that the army and its officers did not have authorities over these issues. The exhibit number 28 is also relevant because it shows that in the combat area, in the zone of combat activities, the army was the one to give permits for the representatives of the civilian protection to enter it. And this is something which is very clear according to all military rules. This is done in order to protect those who entered the area of combat activities and also to protect the deployment of troops and facilities in the area. That is why the army has to give its consent for the movement in the area of combat activities. Since there were some other witnesses who testified on the Prosecution case who objected for not having been given permit to enter the area of combat activities, this is a document that speaks of the authority of the army to give permits for movement in the area of combat activities in order to protect those who move around this area. And finally, document number 34. This document speaks of the issue that has been mentioned by a number of witnesses, and it is the problems that Travnik faced at the time and what measures were put in place in order to help the refugees, the refugees who had arrived from all over the place and lived in very dire conditions. Indirectly, this document also confirms statements that we have heard from the witnesses and it speaks of the situation and how it was compounded by a huge number of witnesses. It speaks of the impossibility to implement all the measures that were ordered. And finally I believe that you have been able to satisfy yourself to the extent to which every single document is relevant for the -- this case and the understanding of the overall situation in June and July 1993. I believe that you have been able to satisfy yourself by listening to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber is going to discuss and the Chamber is going to give you a verbal decision on this issue. May I ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Let me first check whether you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were called -- you have been called as a Defence witness. I would like to ask you first to give me your name, your last name, the date of birth, and the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Salim Tarakcija. I was born on the 22nd of May, 1964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Maline, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated from grammar school. I work in Travnik in the electric distribution ^ and I am an administrative worker in the collection of payment of this company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have a position or did you have a military rank? If this is the case, which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the BiH army in 1992 and in 1993. During that period of time, I was the assistant commander of detachment and later on of the battalion in charge of moral guidance, information, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in which unit or brigade did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you ever testified before an international court or a national court about the -- the things that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you to read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence counsel, I would like to give you a few pieces of information about your testimony. You're going to have to ask -- to answer the questions put to you by the Defence. These questions are normally of neutral nature and should not lead you into responding. After that, you're going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution on your right. The -- their questions are -- will be put to you in order to check your credibility and to clarify some of the answers you gave during the examination-in-chief. Once the Prosecution has finished with their cross-examination, the Defence will have the opportunity to re-examine you to either confirm or check some of the things that you said in response to the questions by the Prosecution. After that, the Judges who are seated in front of you, the three Judges, if there is time and we hope that there will be time, we also want to ask you some questions. The questions put to you by the Judges may Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond differ from the questions put to you by the two parties. Generally speaking, the Judges usually ask questions to clarify things or if there are gaps in your answers, they will ask questions in order to fill those gaps. If the questions are too complicated for you, you may ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it. You can ask -- also ask for our assistance at all times. There are two other things that I warn every witness about. The first one is you have just made a solemn declaration, which means you are not going to give us a false testimony because if you do you may end up in prison or be fined. The second thing I would like to tell you is that if a witness thinks that any statement which he may give us could incriminate him, the Chamber will compel the witness to answer the question, but at the same time the Chamber will give the testimony a certain form of immunity, which means that the answers may never be used against such witness. This is in very general terms what is going to happen during your testimony. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tarakcija.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the words that you have just heard and the warnings by the President -- by the Presiding Judge, I would like to warn you about one more thing. The two of us speak the same language and you will find it easier to answer every question I put to you, however both my question and your answer have to be translated in order to be enable the Judges to understand us and in order for everybody in the courtroom to be able to follow our conversation. That's why I would kindly ask you to make a little pause after my question before giving the answer. Have you understood my words?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Where did you reside on the eve of the war in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I resided in Maline, in the village where I was born. This is a village in Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I finished elementary school in Maline in Guca Gora and then I graduated from grammar school in 1982 in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you serve in the army; and if you did, in which army did you serve?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I served in the former JNA in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time were you given a rank of a sort?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I was a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, do you have a rank today?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I was demobilised from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us about your current profession. Can you please tell us what you did before the war.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Before the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was employed in the company called Sebesic. And it was a timber processing company. I was in charge of the central warehouse of that company.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of war, did you join some Defence forces? If that was the case, can you please tell us which Defence forces were those and where.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: After the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I joined the Territorial Defence. Actually, a unit was established in my native village. It was part of the sector staff of the Territorial Defence. The sector defence was part of the municipal Territorial Defence of Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, I've just been warned that there is a difference between your rank and the interpretation in the English and in French. Can you please tell me again what was the rank that you had when you were demobilised from the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I was captain first class. That is, as a captain first class in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this situation is clear. You said that you had organised yourselves into Territorial Defence units in your village, in Maline. At the time did you assume any duties within your unit?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: For a brief period of time I was the commander of the Maline company which was in the sector staff. And after the Territorial Defence was reorganised, I assumed other duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the Territorial Defence was reorganised in relation to the sector staffs and what duties did you assume.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In June and August 1992, the units of the Territorial Defence were made larger and detachments were formed. Han Bila, Mehurici, Ljuta Greda, and the Hum detachments were formed. I was part of the Hum detachment and I was the assistant commander of the detachment for morale and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the commander of your detachment was at the time.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Salih Softic was the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, what sort of weapons did you have when you formed a company in your village, or rather when you had already formed the detachment?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that you know that before the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the municipality of Travnik and in many other places in Bosnia and Herzegovina, weapons were taken from the Territorial Defence so that the Territorial Defence municipal staff in Travnik wasn't able to arm those involved in the defence and provide them with what they needed to wage a war. So in the area I was deployed in the company, and in the sector staff I was a member of we had very few weapons. We had the weapons that the people had in their villages. On the whole, these weapons were hunting weapons for which they had licenses or perhaps personal weapons, for example, pistols. So we started defending Bosnia and Herzegovina with practically no weapons. And the weapons that people had at the time were placed at the disposal of those who joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tarakcija, could you tell me now since you are from the village of Maline, who the inhabitants living in the area in which you joined the Territorial Defence? And later you were the assistant for morale in Territorial Defence detachment.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, the Hum detachment recruited men and there are six villages covered by that detachment. I think they are Bosnian and Croat villages. These are mixed villages. They are in the vicinity of each other. They are mixed -- there is a mixed population consisting of Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the relations between the Bosniak and Croat inhabitants like before the war when you were still being educated and when you did the work that you have already described?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, the relations were normal, and that was the case in all normal states.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the breakup of Yugoslavia, do you remember there ever being any incidents of a nationalist nature?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any such incidents, and I'm referring to the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reported to the Territorial Defence unit, did the Croatian population also respond to the call-up to join Territorial Defence and what was the situation like in your village?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the beginning of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was obvious that the Croatian population didn't want to join the Territorial Defence, but rather they started forming HVO units in that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond area. This was also the case for the Croatian population in the village in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since -- or rather, before I ask you that question I would like to ask you the following. In the vicinity of your village, was there a village inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The village of Maline is a village in which Bosniaks and Croats live together. It's a mixed village, a village of mixed ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that the Croatian population joined HVO units, were you able to notice at the time how they were armed and equipped when compared to your units?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I've already said that we were poorly armed. But it was obvious that HVO members or almost all its members had the appropriate weapons and equipment. At the beginning of the war, they had infantry weapons and other military equipment. So it wasn't possible to compare the situation we were in with the situation that they were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, at any point in time were other organisational changes introduced within the BH army; and if so, how was your position affected as a result of those changes?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 in December, from the supreme command and the 3rd Corps command in the area in which I was there was an order to form the 306th Mountain Brigade. The detachments I have mentioned were part of this brigade. The Han Bila Detachment was transformed into the 3rd Battalion. Most of the Mehurici detachment was transformed into the 4th Battalion. The Hum Battalion, in which I was in, was transformed into the 2nd Battalion. The 1st so-called Siprage Battalion was formed from the expelled members of the military from Kotor Varos and Skender Vakuf and it was also part of the 306th Mountain Brigade. I was deployed in the 2nd Mountain Battalion, and the assistant commander -- I was the assistant commander for morale and religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command of the 2nd Battalion located?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: It was in the village of Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, who was your commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Fahir Camdzic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the combatants from your 2nd Battalion are concerned, where were they billeted? Did you have a barracks or any other facilities providing combatants with accommodation?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Members of the 2nd Mountain Battalion, if they weren't at the positions facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor mostly spent their time at home. We didn't have barracks of any kind. We didn't have any buildings in which our soldiers could be accommodated after having returned from the defence line. So they were all at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, you said you were the assistant commander for morale and for intelligence and for religious affairs. Can you briefly tell us about the tasks you had when you were performing these duties in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: All the officers involved in morale in units, and that included myself, had to inform the officers about the situation in the zone of responsibility -- in the zone of responsibilities of our units and the brigades and the corps and naturally about the situation of the zone of responsibility of the BH army. That is to say, throughout the battlefield in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Naturally we had to inform officers of efforts made by the politicians to deal with the situation and find a way of bringing the war to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I think one word has been mistranslated. He had "boracki i oficir" -- he said "the combatants and officers," and the translation -- according to the translation only combatants -- only officers were mentioned. I apologise for interrupting you. Could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: We had to inform them about what was happening on the political scene, about the efforts made to put an end to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Furthermore, it was our task to monitor morale in the unit -- the morale of the combatants in order to carry out their tasks. We had to see what was having a bad effect on morale and to suggest to other organs in the units measures that they should take in order to resolve the problems and ensure that the soldiers were motivated to carry out the combat tasks they had. Naturally we suggested that a number of measures be taken, measures that could have a positive effect and would motivate the combatants to carry out their combat tasks. We also had to organise religious practices in the units for those who were religious. And then we had to cooperate with the civilian authorities in the area where our unit was located. And above all, they were to become included in dealing with the positions -- with the problems that the families of some of our combatants had, the families of men who had been killed or handicapped in the course of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of the duties that you have mentioned, how important was it for combatants to be informed about the rules of war and the way of conducting war? Did you have any tasks relating to such matters?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Naturally our superior command and our commanders, it depended on the level, but we received instructions and tasks we were supposed to forward to lower levels, to combatants, and other officers. And we were to inform them about how to conduct themselves when carrying out combat operations. We had to inform them of the international rules of war and we had to make sure that all our members adhered to the basic principles of fighting a war. Above all, it was necessary to inform all combatants that they were to treat the civilian population a humane way, to treat captured soldiers in a humane way. They had to ensure that the property of all the population was protected. And in particular, they had to ensure that the cultural heritage and religious buildings were protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, you said that you completed secondary school. How did you come to know about all the rules you have just mentioned, the rules that you had to inform your soldiers of?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the BH army there were not a sufficient number of professional members, but anyone who wasn't adequately trained but had been assigned duties had the duty to be trained. This occurred at the level of brigades in accordance with corps orders. And in the corps, certain training was organised for officers, too. We had to train and we had to familiarise ourselves with the basic rules. We weren't able to study these matters in a book at the time, but we just had to learn what the basic principles were. We were informed about them. And naturally in the course of the war, if we managed to obtain any literature on this subject, we tried to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were involved, were engaged, in the sector for morale?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: If we're talking about the battalion, apart from the assistant commander of the battalion for morale, intelligence, and religious affairs, there was within the battalion command another position, that of an official for religious affairs. And in each company from the battalion, according to the establishment, there was one officer who was assistant commander of the company for morale and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that one of the tasks you had involved cooperation with the civilian authorities. Could you tell us, in the area of your battalion who were the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In accordance with the decisions of the War Presidency in Travnik municipality, the organisational structure of the local communes was transformed. Some sort of war plans for the local communes in Travnik were formed. And in other areas, there was the Guca Gora local commune which was formed. Representatives of that local commune, in coordination with the War Presidency of Travnik municipality, represented the civilian authorities so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, let's now move on to another subject. At any point in time as a member of the detachment or subsequently as a member of the 2nd Battalion, did you notice that some foreigners were appearing in the Bila Valley area? I'm referring to foreigners who were not from the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. In the second half of 1992, I personally noticed that there were individuals who were not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, passing through or moving around the place I lived in and the other places I have mentioned. We considered them to be foreigners, or rather we could see that they were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, how is it that you could tell they were foreigners and did you know where these foreigners came from?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, given the colour of their skin, the clothes they wore, we could tell that they were foreigners of Arab origin, and it was said that these people had come from Arab countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 did they at any time stay for a certain period of time in your village?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No, they never stayed in the village of Maline. They only passed through Maline, because there's a road from Mehurici to Travnik that passes through Maline. So they just passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you later start calling these Arabs by a different name, and if so, how did you call them?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, at the beginning of 1993, it was said that they were Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where they were accommodated in 1993 when you found out about their presence and later on?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: When they first arrived, I heard that they were staying in the Mehurici primary school. And towards the end of 1992, this is what I heard, they were staying in some houses above the Mehurici settlement and the Poljanice settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the building they were staying in?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No. It was never necessary for me to go in that direction because that was a place that didn't lead to one of our centres. So I never passed through that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an assistant for morale and information, did you at any point in time find out that the presence of these Mujahedin was causing problems in the Bila Valley area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Since they had very little influence in the area where I lived and they weren't staying there, all I can say is what I heard about. I heard that in other places naturally, for example, in Mehurici, there were certain misunderstandings and certain problems, misunderstandings between them and the civilian population or between them and members of our army who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about their attitude towards the civilian population, about their attitude towards religious instruction, about their attitude towards family relations in that area, or did you have any information of any other kind, apart from what you have just told us about now?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I heard that in those areas they had organised religious education for the children of the population. It was said that they were involved in humanitarian activities. They provided clothes, footwear, and other essential items, households. I heard that in the religious buildings they tried -- or in certain religious facilities they tried to introduce a different form of religious rites. They tried to have any other rites in comparison to the rites that were practiced in -- or had been practiced in Bosnia and Herzegovina up until that time. So naturally this caused a lot of misunderstanding and a lot of unease among the population. Because after having prayed for several hundred years in one way if you are then told you have to pray in a different way, it's quite understandable that people didn't feel happy about this. I heard that they would also marry certain girls from those villages, and that also made the situation more difficult. Because when family relations are established of that kind and other inhabitants observe this, this can give rise to even greater misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, let's go -- come back to another issue. You said that the Croatian population joined the HVO. Where were HVO units located with regard to the units of the BiH army that you yourself belonged to in your area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 in the area where my unit was, at the beginning it was the sector staff, later on it was a detachment --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to repeat the year. When was that?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: 1992, after the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: After the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina when the Territorial Defence units were established as well as the HVO units, it was noticeable that the Croatian Defence Council has displayed different behaviour with regard to the Territorial Defence. Truth be told, at that time they shared the same area of responsibility with us on Mount Vlasic facing the Montenegrin-Serbian aggressor. However, their positions were never on the front line. They were never at the same level. They were always behind our backs, so to speak, and we were often in the position to control the area of responsibility on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident which took place in the Lasva Valley which had a bearing on the situation in the area of responsibility of the 306th Brigade and your battalion? Did these incidents have any bearing on the behaviour of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993 when in Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and Vitez there were clashes between the HVO and the BiH army. These conflicts had an impact on the situation in Travnik municipality and the area of responsibility of our battalion. The Croatian Defence Council was no longer behaving the way they behaved at the beginning of 1992 and in the course of that year. They started controlling the free territory in Travnik municipality and the territory where the 2nd Mountain Battalion was deployed. They started putting up checkpoints. They started controlling all those who wanted to pass through their checkpoints from the villages towards Travnik and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This type of behaviour on the part of HVO, the checkpoints and the attitude towards individuals at those checkpoints, did this have any impact on the morale of your men and what did you do in order to suppress tensions and prevent possible conflicts?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Obviously whatever was happening at the checkpoints, the humiliation that our members experienced at those checkpoints, did have an impact on the overall situation in the unit. Obviously our task was to talk to our men on a daily basis. We tried to tell them that these problems should be overcome, that we shouldn't be the ones who would retaliate after such incidents. We shouldn't allow for a conflict to break out with the HVO. In Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, it was not a normal -- it was not to be expected that a second theatre of war would be opened, since there was already one against the Serbs and the Montenegrins. We had enough problems. We didn't want to create any new ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, did the HVO appreciate those efforts? Did they stop creating situations which might lead to the deterioration of the situation in the general area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the level of the brigade command, pursuant to the orders of the corps command, I know that a commission was established and it was a joint commission with the HVO. The task of this commission was to seek ways in order to overcome problems. This commission did try to reach an agreement on dealing with the problem. They wanted to see how these checkpoints could be removed and to -- and how the free territory would be free for everybody. This was all aimed at fighting the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. The joint commission was supposed to go from one checkpoint to another, later on from one trench to another, from one settlement to another. And the task of this commission was to plead with those who had dug out those trenches to fill them in and to plead with the people to try and find us a solution to the problem. However, the situation was really bad and whatever the commission agreed would not be implemented. It -- every measure was very short-lived and it lasted only for a few hours or just a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, did this behaviour result in deaths? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: During the period when there was still no open conflicts with the HVO, there were no casualties at the checkpoints. Earlier on, I believe that it was on the 16th of April, 1993, which was the time when we still did not have an open conflict with the HVO in the area of responsibility of our battalion, on the 16th of April, a fighter from Maline was killed in the shooting that took place on a line. This was an uncontrolled shooting on the line between Maline and Guca Gora. That is when one man got killed. Later on what happened at this checkpoint was that people were taken into custody, they were beaten, property was seized from people, their cars would be confiscated. This is what happened before the open conflict broke out with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us in very general terms what was happening. Were you familiar with any of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the month of March, there was a gradual blockade which culminated in the month of May. The population in the villages that I've mentioned came under a blockade. I remember that in mid-May two things happened that involved my family. One of my cousins was arrested in Guca Gora. He was beaten up. And one person from Guca Gora snatched him from the military police of the HVO, transported him to the far end of the village of Guca Gora. That person called Salih Softic and asked Salih to come and pick him up and transport him to the hospital. That's one case. Another case which happened later on was when some people were returning from Travnik and my uncle's car was stopped at a checkpoint. And my father and a cousin of mine were in the car. The car was stopped very close to the monastery in Guca Gora. At gunpoint, my father, my cousin, and my uncle were driven out of the car. They took away the car and all the food that they had bought in Travnik. All this was taken away. My father, my late father, had been shot at and a burst of fire was opened at him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, you said that in May the situation became really difficult and that the villages were completely blocked. In May of that year, what was the situation in your battalion? Where were the troops of that battalion deployed?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The situation at the battalion was very difficult. This battalion was replenished from the six settlements, namely Maline, Krpeljici, Mosor, Bandol, Radojcici and Velika Bukovica. Once the villages were blocked we could no longer replenish our battalion and we could no longer communicate, let alone carry out our combat tasks. We could not have the changeover of troops on the lines. The battalion command was not in one place. The battalion commander was in Krpeljici and the rest of the command staff were in their respective settlements where they were born and where they resided. The system of command and control was not in place. It was not functioning -- actually, it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your village? Was your village blocked? Was it able to communicate with other parts of the battalion and the command?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In mid-May my village was blocked. After the incidents that I have just mentioned there was a total blockade of Maline as well as of all the other villages from which the 2nd Mountain Battalion was replenished. We were not able to communicate with the rest of the troops from this battalion. All of us who were members of the 2nd Battalion were mostly billeted in Maline and we did not have any means of communications with the others. Some of our troops were on the line on Mount Vlasic and they did not have the possibility to come to Maline. We were not in a position to send them relief. We did not have the possibility to send them food or anything else up to the line where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of June 1993 did you manage to get to your command post or were you still in Maline, the village that was encircled?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At the beginning of June 1993 I was not in contact with the commander. None of us who were members of the command could go to the command post. We could not communicate with our superior commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were at home. Where were the HVO positions? What weapons did they have at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: HVO soldiers occupied most of the prominent facilities around Maline. They held the line from the direction of Guca Gora, from Gornje Maline, and from Postinje. So we were almost fully encircled. The only thing we could do, although it wasn't very safe, we could get to Han Bila. That was the only settlement which was accessible, although it could not be done safely because the -- that area was also controlled by the HVO. We could go along the Bila River and get to Han Bila. This was the only access that was accessible to us. Han Bila was also circled on other axes. We were not able to communicate with any other settled areas. Nobody from those settled areas was in a position to reach us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the commander of your battalion at that time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: He was in Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was going on with the troops in other places from which your battalion was replenished, Velika Bukovica, Bandol, Radojcici, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The situation was very similar, as in Maline. The troops were in their settlements and they organised the defence of their respective settlements, just as we did in Maline. Later on the Croatian Defence Council launched an attack on Velika Bukovica and I assume that you're aware of what happened there. The first village that the Croatian Defence Council attacked at the beginning of June was Velika Bukovica. Later on an attack was launched against the village of Radojcici. And later on there would also be an attack on Maline and on Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about the situation in Velika Bukovica?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 6th of June. I believe that it was on the 6th of June, from the direction of Guca Gora a woman came to Maline. Her family name was Suljic. I can't remember her first name. She came to Maline and she asked to be received by somebody from the command in Maline. Obviously I was the one to conduct an interview with that woman. And in the conversation with this woman - and there was just another man from Maline who was present - I could see on her face that something terrible had happened in Velika Bukovica. That's why I didn't want anybody else to be present during that conversation. That's why I held this conversation in the presence of only one person. I believe that he was her cousin. After that conversation I learned from her that she had been brought to Guca Gora by her neighbour from Velika Bukovica, that he sent her from Guca Gora to Maline, and the task that he gave her was to inform -- to try and get in touch with the troops from Velika Bukovica who had managed to flee from Bukovica on the eve of the HVO attack. The objective was a possible exchange. What she told us was that a crime had been committed in Velika Bukovica, that Velika Bukovica had been completely torched and destroyed. She said that some seven to nine people had been killed. She could not provide us with the precise data. She also told us that the civilian population had been gathered in one place by the HVO. She also told us that one child had arrived from a place called Konjska and that this child had been sent by the soldiers from Velika Bukovica who had managed to escape. And as they were walking on that axis they captured some of the Croatian inhabitants. And the child that was among those people, they sent it to Velika Bukovica in order to warn the HVO soldiers not to commit any crimes over civilian population. And this Croatian child informed the HVO soldiers that there were some Croatian prisoners and that these people had been taken towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were you in a position to check this information? Secondly, were you in a position to assist Velika Bukovica in any way?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: This was the first such case in this area, the case of such an atrocious crime. I found it very hard to understand what had happened. And this woman, she was also scared, she was terrified. None of us could understand or appreciate what had happened. We were not in a position to check this information and we were not in a position to extend any help to those who were in Velika Bukovica. We ourselves were encircled in Maline, and it was not possible for us to send any of the troops there. And we had an obligation to defend Maline. But let me just say that at that time I insisted that the person who had informed us about the incident and with Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the person who was present during our conversations not to spread this news in order to prevent possible panic among the population in Maline. We had our line facing the Croatian population there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned an attack on your village that took place later on. Can you please describe what happened and who was it who launched this attack.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: On the following day, the day after we learned about Velika Bukovica, on the 7th of June Maline was attacked from the positions of the HVO. It was an infantry attack from the positions. During that attack we suffered some consequences. One man was slightly injured. Three cowsheds burned to the ground and three houses were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 8th of June, 1993? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, in the early morning hours I was in Maline together with the troops and the civilian population. In the early morning hours there was shooting along the entire length of the line facing the HVO. At that time we didn't know what this was all about. This shooting came from all sides. After some time, maybe half an hour or an hour of this shooting we saw that on the northern side of the line in the direction of Mehurici the shooting had stopped. And that -- in that area the HVO had stopped putting up resistance. This is a rock called Vranjaca and we could see the BiH army troops descending that rock and moving towards the village. We were tasked to send the men from Maline towards Guca Gora, towards the western and southern sides of the line. This task was given to us by the battalion commander because in the meantime the blockade had been lifted from Krpeljici. This was our task. This is the order that we received via Bandol. Bandol had still been putting up resistance against the HVO. They were still fighting. We did not have a direct communication with the battalion commander. He managed to send a message to us via the communication hub in Bandol. Bandol was the scene of fierce fighting. We were told to direct our forces towards Guca Gora and link up with the troops from Krpeljici and the troops of the 3rd Mountain Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, maybe this would be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will still need about 20 minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We shall resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll resume now. I'll give the floor to Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, before the break you said that you received an order from your battalion commander to head off in the direction of Guca Gora and try to link up the forces with other parts of the battalion. Tell me, where did you and the soldiers go the following days and which positions did you finally reach and when did you reach them?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: After we had linked up the lines on the 8th of June in the afternoon hours and at night, we linked up the lines with the Krpeljici soldiers and soldiers of the 3rd Battalion on the Han Bila axis. After having done that we remained on the lines we had reached above Guca Gora. We were there on the following day, too. It was only after the population of Guca Gora had left Guca Gora and after the HVO soldiers who were defending Guca Gora had left their positions. It was on the 10th of June that we received the task to move our forces in the village of Radojcici in the direction of Mosor [Realtime transcript read in error "Mostar"]. The direct I have was to liberate the village of Bandol and essentially control Radojcici. Since the Bosniak population from the village of Radojcici had also left their village and they had fled in the direction of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, did you and your soldiers pass through Guca Gora or did you go to those positions via some other route?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In Maline we received the task to go with combatants from Maline partly in the direction of Mosor, and partly in the direction of Radojcici. Some were to go in one direction and some in the other. I went in the direction of Mosor with other soldiers. We were to establish defence lines towards the HVO at the Gostunj place. That is to say by the village of Mosor. I only passed through Guca Gora on the 10th or the 11th of June, I think. We went there in vehicles. We went to the direction of Mosor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, on that occasion -- or first of all, I'd like to ask you whether on the 8th and 9th you noticed that any houses had been burned or destroyed in the part of Maline in which the population was Croatian.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the course of combat on the 8th of June a number of buildings in Gornje Maline, which is where the Croatian population lived, were burned. I noticed them burning. I couldn't say how many buildings were affected since there was shooting from all sides as I have already said. But in the course of the combat, some residential buildings and other buildings in the part of the village which was Croatian were damaged and burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you entered Gornje Maline -- when did you enter Gornje Maline for the first time after those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I think after 20 or 25 days' time I was able to leave the defence lines and return to my village. I had enough time then to visit Gornje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a correction on page 33, line 23. The witness said "in the direction of Mosor," whereas the transcript says in the direction of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you drove through Guca Gora, tell me, on that occasion, did you notice that any buildings in Guca Gora had been burned, damaged, or destroyed in some other way?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I'd just like to correct something you said. I drove through in a TAM vehicle with combatants who were with me. I was with my driver. We passed through -- we drove through Guca Gora. We headed in the direction of Guca Gora -- in the direction of Mosor. I couldn't see much because this was just a road through Guca Gora. And on that occasion I couldn't notice any damaged objects, any damaged buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness Defence Exhibit 1214. It's number 9 in the list of documents that we referred to earlier. Before we show you this document, could you tell me whether the village of Postinje is part of Donje Maline or is it a different village?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: This is a separate village. It's part of the local commune of -- in Maline. That was the case before the war and that's the case now after the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many houses, as far as you know, were there in Gornje Maline in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I can't say exactly but I think there were no more than a hundred houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now have a look at the document before you. Under item 1 reference is made to a name from Donje Maline. Could you first have a look to see whether these names mean anything to you. Do they remind you of any of the inhabitants of Gornje or Donje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In this document the names are names of inhabitants of Donje and Gornje Maline. I can see that inhabitants of the village of Postinje are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the first five names. Tell me, what is the nationality of these people?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: These people are Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Further on it says that the incident took place on the 7th of June, 1993, as mentioned next to each name. Tell me, what does this mean for you? What does this mean to you? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, I have said that Maline was attacked by the HVO on the 7th of June. What's referred to here is something that happened in the HVO attack in the village and at our positions in Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you -- when you had a look at the names you said that the village of Postinje is also mentioned. When you have a look at this list, could you tell me which individuals from that other village or which buildings from the other village are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: These are the buildings under the name Balta Mato, Balta Ivo, and Balta Vesko. They are all from the village of Postinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a quick look at the other names, the remaining 15 names, could you tell us whether these people are from Gornje Maline, if you can recognise these names.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The family names here show that all these people are from Gornje Maline because I know that people who had such a family name were from Gornje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at one of the items. Under item 14, Mijo Juric. Is that family name from Gornje Maline that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 under item 14 it says that the police arrived at the site immediately and tried to identify the perpetrator but couldn't find the perpetrator. Mr. Tarakcija, if a building was set afire, do you know what kind of measures were taken at the time in such cases?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: When this sort of thing happened, those who had control of the territory left by Croats were the civilian police. They had to provide security for the buildings in those settlements. It was their task to establish their identity of the perpetrators, to establish the identity of those who had set fire or destroyed certain buildings. And it was their task to take the legally prescribed measures against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, could you please have a look at the last page on this document. The date is the 21st of August, 1993. I don't know if you've managed to read the description next to each name, but to the best of your recollection at that time would this report reflect the situation such as it was in Gornje Maline at the end of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Since I've only had a brief glance at this document, please give me a little more time. I think that the document, such as it is, accurately reflects the situation in the settlements and the state of the buildings in the settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, since you were there later on in 1993 and you were there after the conflict with the HVO, you've been there since that conflict ended right up until today, tell me, after 1993 were any buildings damaged for various reasons or were any buildings in this village that was abandoned destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Naturally after 1993, some buildings that hadn't been damaged or destroyed in the course of combat were damaged. Some individuals whose identity was established by the civilian police committed such acts. I don't know how many such individuals were detected and I don't know what measures were taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you are an inhabitant of Maline, you're familiar with any parts of houses being stolen, roofs, doors, et cetera, and are you familiar with any such cases after the end of the war, that is to say after 1995?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I couldn't say that there were such cases and I can't say that there weren't any such cases. I can only guess as to what happened during that period. But that would not be of any relevance for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Document P87 now be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't think it contains any information that would reveal the identity of the witness who presented this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I'll check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will conceal the handwritten parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the names of individuals should be concealed. The drawing should not be concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what we have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, could you have a look at all of these images and could you say whether you recognise this place, although it says which place it is. Could you tell me whether you recognise the place.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: This is Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see a lot of arrows. If these arrows represented the damaged buildings in Gornje Maline in 1993, would you say that the number of buildings that are referred to reflects the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I don't think this is an accurate reflection of the situation. This is in contradiction with the document we mentioned a while ago. In that document we have the civilian protection report on buildings damaged during the period concerned. And I think that in the course of combat action at that period, these buildings were not all damaged on that occasion. Some buildings were probably damaged after that period and perhaps after the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tarakcija. You can return this document to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Using the photos, could the witness indicate the location of his house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. President, you can't see all of Donje Maline in this photograph, so I cannot indicate the location of my house. I'm referring to photograph number 1, Maline number 1. And part of the Bosniak settlement can be seen in that photograph. This is just one of the hamlets in Maline. So you can't see the part of Maline which is where the house I live in is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And in photograph Maline 2, can you see your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. These buildings are buildings in which Croats lived. This is the Croatian part of the Maline settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about Maline 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This also shows part of the settlement in which Croats lived, but there is a small area in which Bosniaks lived, too. In the area marked by number 44, there's a school building there, a number of other buildings in which Bosniaks lived. These buildings were in the immediate vicinity of buildings in which Croats lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about Maline 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croats lived in these buildings. This is a part in the direction of Guca Gora and I can also notice the Catholic cemetery here. The part of Maline I live in is far away. It's closer to the Bila River. It's at some distance from the part of the settlement in which Croats lived. Maline is not a small village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that in the part that you lived in -- you're saying that the part that you lived in cannot be seen in the four photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, after the war did your neighbours from Gornje Maline return and move back into their houses?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, but not to the extent that one expected this to happen. I think that about 20 families returned to Gornje Maline and up to 10 families returned to the village of Postinje, which was part of this local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of relation do you have with those neighbours who have returned?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Given everything that happened during the period we've been referring to, it would be no exaggeration to say that the situation is normal now. And those that have returned to Gornje Maline are on normal terms with Bosniaks in Maline, and they cooperate with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any incidents involving Bosniaks who might have done something unpleasant to your Bosniak neighbours since the time they returned up until today?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of any incidents from the time that they started returning to Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked together. Do you have any joint projects or do the inhabitants of Gornje and Donje Maline work in a normal way, do they establish normal professional relationships and friendships?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, after some of these people returned to Maline, as I said, a joint organ of the local commune in Maline was formed. And representatives of the Bosniaks and Croats take decisions together in order to solve certain problems in that area, especially problems that concern the infrastructure. We're involved in a number of projects. We're cooperating on the construction of a water supply system. We asphalted certain roads for the Postinje area. So we tried to reach agreements on things of common interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tarakcija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions to clarify some of Mr. Tarakcija's answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tarakcija, at the beginning of your testimony you said that you were the assistant commander for morale and information?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: According to that establishment post that you had, did you also have to deal with religious affairs within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, it was also our task to organise religious life within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the battalion there was an officer for religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this officer?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Grabus Nurija, Efendi Grabus Nurija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the 306th and the brigade command, did they also have a post for an officer of religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, they did have an official for religious affairs at the level of the brigade command. There was no such establishment post. These tasks were carried out by the assistant for morale with other officers who had been given such posts according to the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What were the tasks of the officer for religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: His tasks in accordance with the orders from the commander and instructions provided by the assistant commander for morale were to organise religious life in accordance with the circumstances at the time. This was for those who were religious.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If we examine the ethnic composition of your battalion, the battalions were all Muslim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, let's now go back to the 8th of June. When you were answering questions put to you by Ms. Residovic, on a number of occasions you said "our forces," and you said the 3rd Battalion. You meant members of the 306th Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to forces of the 306th Mountain Brigade, because in the course of that combat operation only men from the 306th Brigade were engaged. It was also our task to link up our forces with the 3rd Mountain Battalion from the 306th Brigade. And their headquarters were located in Han Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the territory in which men were engaged so there weren't any other units there from the BH army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin and I am one of the Prosecutors representing the Prosecutor in this case. As the President of the Trial Chamber indicated to you I am going to ask you a few questions based on what you said to us this afternoon. If at any time you do not understand my questions or you wish for me to repeat any part of it, feel free to do so and I'll oblige. Thank you. Now, maybe we should start with the last spot first, the last section of your examination-in-chief. And you told us that you were born in Maline and that you lived all your life in Maline. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I just gathered that you were from Donje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us the population of Donje Maline.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: It was mostly Bosniaks that inhabited Donje Maline and that still inhabit Donje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And how much in number would that be?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Approximately up to a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And Gornje Maline, I believe you said that was the part that was inhabited by the Croats. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us approximately how many inhabitants there might have been in Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, not more than 600. And this figure also covers the inhabitants of Postinje which we always consider part of Maline, although it's a small hamlet inhabited by Croats only. So to sum it up, according to the 1991 census, the part, the Croatian part of Maline and Postinje had up to 600 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would I be correct in saying that the two villages Donje Maline and Gornje Maline lie side by side, they are adjacent to each other. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: We consider this one village because they are adjacent to each other. But for an easier understanding and for the purpose of understanding the national breakup, we divide it into Gornje and Donje Maline.
