However, it was obvious from the photos that you have just shown me, this is just one village and Croatian and Muslim parts even intermingle at places.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So then would I be correct in saying that anything that goes on in Gornje Maline, the people in Donje Maline would be very much aware?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: They don't necessarily have to know everything. However, it is possible that they are aware of the more significant things. We cannot be aware of all the details of everything that is going on in any one house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You were quite right when you said the more significant details, because that's what I was speaking of, that's what I was referring to. Now, on the 8th of June, 1993, you testified that Maline - and I take it to be Donje and Gornje Maline - was encircled by the HVO. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: You are not correct. The HVO encircled Donje Maline. Just one part of Maline which we identify as Donje Maline. The part of Maline inhabited by the Bosniaks. This part was encircled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So in answer to my learned friend on page 28, line 10, of this transcript when you said that the HVO occupied most prominent facilities around Maline, is that what you are referring to, Donje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The most prominent facilities around Maline. When I say "Maline," I mean Donje and Gornje Maline. The HVO also had a line in the village between the houses towards Donje Maline. Their line was in the direction towards Mehurici. They could control every house in Donje and Gornje Maline. But they also had their defence line between the Bosniak and Croatian houses in the village itself on the contact point between these two rows of houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, if I were to say to you that witnesses have appeared before this Trial Chamber and have indicated in their testimony that the village of Maline was under control of the BH army, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know what was the context when the witnesses said that. The part of Maline that we call Donje Maline inhabited by Bosniaks was under the control of the BH army, i.e., the part of the 2nd Mountain Battalion which was in the village of Maline at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. I think that we are referring here to the period that you were discussing, which would have been about June of 1993. And hence, that is what the witness or witnesses might have been referring to as well, that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask my learned friend, since she has mentioned witnesses saying something, it would be fair to say to the witness who and when said what, otherwise she's just confusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Henry-Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend knows very well that that is not possible and that I couldn't do it. And I think my learned friend herself in this very court has indicated to witnesses that witnesses have come forward and said and alleged certain things. And it's based on that that I'm putting it to this witness. And I'm sorry, I would not be calling any witnesses' names here, especially since some of the witnesses are protected witnesses. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us the size of the army or the size of your battalion in Maline at the time.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The part of the battalion who was in Maline at the time numbered up to 120 men at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to tell us if the HVO army was larger than yours or was smaller than yours at that time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know how many troops the HVO had. But I know that the HVO unit were linked up and there was the Frankopan Brigade which was linked up with Guca Gora and with other Croatian settlements on both sides. I am not in a position to say anything about their numbers, but bearing in mind what they had at their disposal and compared to what we had, I believe that they had a considerable advantage. And obviously one has to bear in mind the territory that they had occupied around every settlement. I am saying that they had a considerable advantage over us who were encircled by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If you had to compare the size of both armies, which would you say was the larger army?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Since I've mentioned the Frankopan Brigade of the HVO in the territory of Guca Gora, and when you compare that with the battalion and if you understand the difference between a battalion and a brigade, then you will understand who had the advantage. If you have a battalion on the one hand facing a brigade on the other hand, and if you bear in mind that that battalion was decimated and broken up in several places, then the difference is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let us go to the 8th of June in particular, 1993. And you were based in Maline, as you told us. Could you clarify for the Trial Chamber and myself if you are aware of anything significant that may have taken place with respect to Croat civilians in Maline in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. Do you want me to speak only about the 8th of June or the entire month of June? Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sorry. I think I mentioned the 8th of June specifically. Are you aware of any incident with respect to Croat civilians, involving Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the late afternoon hours, together with the other battalion officers, I was linking up with the Krpeljici and the 3rd Battalion. I received information that the civilian population -- the Croatian civilian population from Gornje Maline had left -- had been taken towards Mehurici. And a few of them -- only a few of them had remained in Maline, maybe two or three families all together on that specific day. And this happened in the late afternoon hours. This is when I learned that most of the population had been taken in the direction of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll be a little more specific so we can move on. During your tenure in Maline and in particular on the 8th of June, were you aware of any massacre of any Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June I was not aware of any such case. Something happened in Bikose. Bikose is part of Maline. I learned about that four or five days later. I heard what was being said on the defence line facing the HVO. But it was only four or five days later. On that particular day I didn't know what was going on or what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as commander or assistant commander for morale, did you think it prudent that you should investigate it?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I did not have to give it a second thought. I knew that the investigation had been carried out by the security department at the level of the brigade. I myself was never informed about the results of that investigation. Obviously as a human being I thought, I believed that such an incident had to be investigated, that perpetrators had to be detected and punished. I was an officer, but I was not in charge of that. We had another officer who was in charge of security who was in charge of such investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague showed you a document -- a Defence Document 1214. And with the permission of the Trial Chamber if I can just have the document given back to the witness. I need to clarify a few ... If you look at page 2 of the document you quite rightly said to us that the majority of the names on that document would have been Croat civilians. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I am not aware of Croat soldiers, civilians. I don't make a distinction. I did say that these were Croatian names, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Croatian names. And if you look at the conclusion, it's usually in the last sentence, as to the causes of the fire or the looting, could you tell us basically what was the general assessment.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Could you please clarify. Do you want me to draw a conclusion based on this document or do you want me to provide comment to the conclusion that already exists at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No. I do not want you to draw a conclusion. In fact I think I was quite clear when I asked you if you could just point out for me what conclusion was arrived at. It's usually on the last line of each paragraph. And if you wish, I can help you. In some instances it says that it was just burned to the ground. Nobody said how it was set. In some instances they said they couldn't find out how the fire was set, not knowing who set the fire. So in fact there was never a conclusion as to what caused this fire. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what it says at the end of the document, this is a conclusion by those who drafted this document, my comment would be that during the combat that took place on the 8th of June in that place, it would not have been realistic to expect anybody to identify how houses were burned because shooting came from all sides, from the positions of the HVO as well as from the position of the BH army. This might point to a conclusion that these buildings could have been set on fire from both sides, from the side of the HVO as well as from the side of the BiH army. This would be my comment and this is the conclusion I would arrive at.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I'd like you to look at the front page, page 1. And if you look at, let's say, paragraph 1 to 3, I -- it says that the houses were based or the individuals were from Donje Maline. So I take it that these individuals might have been Bosniaks. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if you look at the conclusion for these, in each instance it says that the HVO -- the fire was caused or it was set alight from HVO positions on the top of the rock in each instance. And if we go right down, on each instance it gives the cause of the fire basically from the HVO's positions. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, in light of that, won't you agree with me that it is very strange that the houses in Gornje Maline which were destroyed, that no one can find a reason why these houses were destroyed? But for the houses in Donje Maline, there was a definite reason. Would you agree with me if I say that something seems a little amiss there? Bearing in mind that you did say that the fire was coming from either side, so that really no one really knows which side caused which, bearing in mind that.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Let me clarify. On the 7th of June, the HVO forces attacked the village of Maline. From their positions directly, as it's described herein, they shot at various buildings and I suppose that it suffices to provide this argument in order to claim this. It was not the BiH army that shot at the buildings that they were providing security for. What you are trying to compare, obviously you are drawing a conclusion from something that somebody else drafted. You should know that on the 8th of June, there was no -- the HVO positions were not shot at only from Donje Maline. The 306th Mountain Brigade opened fire from Mehurici on the positions of the HVO above Maline. We're talking about combat operations which were different than the ones on the 7th of June when the HVO had launched an attack on our positions on the buildings that we were providing security for. Obviously you would have a much clearer picture if you had an opportunity to visit the place to have the deployment of forces explained to you. Then you would be much clearer on the whole situation. What happened on the 7th of June was totally different to what happened on the 8th of June. We didn't only try to defend ourselves, we also tried to make a breakthrough in order to help the population in Bukovica who had experienced atrocities. And that's when shooting started from all sides because we were engaged in a mutual showdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But with all due respect to you, sir, and in interests of time, not only has the 7th of June been mentioned but the 8th of June has been mentioned on the first page and on the last page the 6th of June has been mentioned. So with all due respect to you, I don't think your conclusion is pretty correct. And I'm only going by the document that is before me; that's all I have to go by. But I ask you that to say this now, as I said to you, witnesses have come before this court and have testified that the BiH army soldiers were in control of the village of Maline and that their village or their houses were set on fire then. And I'm asking you this question in light of the document 1214 and in light of the fact that all the ones that appear on page --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a while ago I objected to the way the question was put to the witness. There was no need for me to respond to the comment provided by my learned friend because she rephrased her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, she responded to your objection. You said that if the Prosecution made a reference to the facts that were mentioned by a witness, then the Prosecution should mention the name of the witness and the facts mentioned. But the Prosecution responded that the witness was a protected witness and that they couldn't make a specific reference before this witness to a protected witness. This was their response to your objection. They said that there was a statement by the witness but they didn't provide any details. Is that what you wanted to hear?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that if one of the parties wants to provide a counter-argument to say something contrary to what the witness is saying, then because of the facts that they are mentioning and rather than for the names, it would be important and fair to provide those facts to the witness. If we are facing the problem of a protected witness, in that case the names and the facts should be mentioned either in private session or the witness should be referred by the pseudonym that was given to him during the testimony. This is only in the case when counter-arguments are provided, and I maintain my position that in the cross-examination a witness should not be in the position to have to reply to the questions put in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that my learned friend has forgotten that this is cross-examination, one. Secondly, if she wants me to put it a different way, I can put it. I can tell the witness that there is evidence before this court and we will continue on that leg. But there is absolutely nothing wrong in telling the witness that there is evidence before the court to the contrary. There is absolutely nothing wrong with it. And I would ask the Court to allow me to proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, there is evidence before this Court that in Maline on the 8th of June, 1993, that the BH army soldiers was in control -- the village of Maline was under the control of the BH army. And I draw your attention to Defence document 1214 because it appears to me that it is agreeing with the evidence that is before the Court. Page 2 clearly has an exhaustive list of houses that were destroyed during that period. But page 2 of the document for some reason was not able to say the cause of the destruction. Yet, on page 1 we are able to see the cause of destruction. And my question to you was: Don't you think that the evidence that is led before the Court might be correct in the sense that the BH army was in fact the army that was under control -- that had control of Maline during that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase this question for the witness because it's a very long question and perhaps the witness has lost his bearings. The question is as follows: The Prosecution believes on the basis of various forms of evidence that the BH army had control over Maline. And the Prosecution wants to know what your opinion is of that subject. Is it true? False? Is it just partially true? What is your position because we know that you were in Maline? You were there in several capacities. You were an inhabitant of Maline and you were a member of the military there, too. So what do you think about this? The Prosecution claims that they have evidence according to which Maline was under BH army control. So the Prosecution is asking a member of the military, like yourself, to express his opinion. What do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of June, Maline wasn't under the control of the BH army for the entire day. From the early morning hours until about noon, there were clashes, there was fighting in that area. If I have understood your question correctly, it was only in the afternoon hours that one might say that Gornje and Donje Maline were under the control of the BH army. Our forces were moved towards the positions in the direction of Guca Gora. This is something we have already mentioned. That's how I understand the situation. On the 8th of June, Gornje Maline, which is a part of Maline, wasn't under the control of the BH army for the entire day. If we're relating this to the documents we have before us, I'm referring to the combat operation on the 8th of June in the early morning hours. These operations took place in the narrow area of Maline for a few hours. And then the focus of operations was moved towards the lines of the HVO in the direction of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. With respect to your role as assistant commander for morale, you indicated to my learned friend that you -- your superior was the commander. And my question to you now is: Whose superior was that commander? Who did that commander report to?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: To the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Which would have been the 306th Brigade. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with who was the ultimate superior? Who was the superior of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: According to the system of command and control, he would have been the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us who was the corps commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think Mr. Hadzihasanovic was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was the overall commander of the 3rd Corps, and so ultimately responsible for the 3rd Corps. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before I give you the floor, did the question concern military responsibility, disciplinary responsibility, criminal responsibility? Before the Defence objects to your question, could you be a little more specific because it is ambiguous. If you ask whether the 3rd Corps commander was responsible, what do you mean exactly? Responsible for what? I noticed that Defence counsel was about to object. So rephrase your question, please, and be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And first I will ask you if the 3rd Corps commander was responsible militarily. Did he have military responsibility for the members of the corps? Did he?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: According to the system of command and control in the BH army, the corps commander was the commander of the brigade commanders unless there was some sort of operations group that had been formed. But naturally this would have been done in accordance with orders issued by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier on in your testimony you had indicated to my learned friend that the army of which you were a member, the Bosnian army, and in particular the 306th Muslim [sic] Brigade, that you had little or no weapons within which to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, as assistant commander for morale, could you tell me what was the plan then by the ABiH for defending Bosnia and Herzegovina, in light of the fact that you said that you had little or no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there was an error on page 35, line 19. It says the 306th Muslim Brigade here. I don't know if that's what my learned colleague said. Perhaps she was referring to the Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that's what I said. Sorry. 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I noticed that that's what you said when listening to the interpretation, but my answer is as follows. The 306th Mountain Brigade and all the other BH army units naturally organised its defence on the basis of its possibilities. It used the materiel and technical equipment that it had to organise its defence. As to how successful they were in doing this, well naturally it's not necessary for me to address that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the same thing you indicated that it was quite obvious that the HVO members or units had the appropriate weapons. And could I ask you on what premise did you base this? What was your basis for saying this?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: This was said on the basis of what I could observe. I was able to observe the units, the units that were equipped and that were at the defence lines at the beginning of 1992. There were positions on Vlasic. So I made this claim on the basis of what I had observed and on the basis of information I had obtained from others.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You were responsible for training as well. And my question to you is: Were there other trainers or people who train members of the army in the BiH army. Do you know if any other people trained members in the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: According to an order from the superior command, in all brigades according to the establishment there was an operations and training organ whose task was to draw up plans for training. And together with other officers from subordinate units, they were to train men for all aspects of combat readiness. There were plans, there were persons responsible to implement these plans, these were meant for the operations and training organ on the whole, and they would conduct the training in the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you happen to know and if you can, can you please assist the Trial Chamber, would you happen to know if the foreigners, and as you later referred to them, the Mujahedins, would you happen to know if they held training sessions for members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with such cases. In the unit that I was in, in the area that I was in, they did not hold training sessions of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you know if -- maybe you can assist us. Do you know if there was a training camp in Mehurici by these foreign people, the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I heard about the existence of a camp. I mentioned a location of the camp. I heard that training was conducted there with some individuals who had joined them. I heard that some individuals who had joined them were being trained there, but I didn't observe this myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as part of your duty to deal with morale and to monitor morale in the units, first could you tell me if you were aware of Muslim foreigners integrated into your unit.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No. There were never Muslim foreigners engaged in our unit. There were no foreigners from other states either.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How did you deal with the morale of the soldiers in your unit? How did you go about dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The question is a very general one and I can give you a general answer. My task and the task of all officers as something I have already mentioned was to continually monitor everything that had an effect on combat morale in our unit. We had to monitor elements that had a positive and negative effect on morale. Through other organs in the brigade, we had to try and remove elements that had a negative effect on morale. We had to emphasise what might have a positive effect on the morale of the men when carrying out a combat task. So that's the only sort of answer I can give you in response to the type of general question you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In light of the fact that you were so deeply involved in the training and the morale aspect of it, in your area of responsibility, did you find or did you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to the part of the question in which my learned colleague says that he was deeply involved in training. In his testimony so far the witness never said that he was involved in the training. He described his tasks and the training plan that was drafted in the brigade and that was carried out by the individuals referred to in the training plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We will go back to the morale aspect of it then and tell me in your opinion, did you come across soldiers with low morale, soldiers -- or did you come across incidents of soldiers who had to be treated for low morale, in particular soldiers who may have been committing offenses on the outside? Did you come across any such instances?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: We have to make a distinction between combat morale and the morale that you are talking about. I was speaking about the combat morale of BH army members, or rather men in my unit. I was talking about how motivated they were to carry out combat tasks. I wasn't speaking about their moral qualities as people or about their readiness to commit immoral acts. But naturally, when attempting to ensure that combat morale was at an adequate level, we tried to explain to our soldiers that they should behave in a moral way when involved in combat tasks and when involved in operations of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered the question quite rightly, because I thought both -- there was a nexus between both in order for it to operate properly. Now, my question has to do now with the foreigners who came through Maline. And could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber explain to us or enlighten us as to what was the response in Maline to the foreigners who came through Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At one point you mentioned the foreigners who came to Maline. I said that I and other people who lived in Maline only had the opportunity of occasionally seeing foreigners passing through Maline and heading in the direction of Travnik. Since they weren't active in the area that I lived in, we can't really speak about population reacting to them in any particular way in the area that I lived in and in the area where we recruited men into the unit. So they passed through the settlement that I lived in at the time, and the area in which I was a member of the unit I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I ask you this because you say -- earlier on you indicated that the HVO was the army that was in control of Maline in June of 1993. And I ask you this question was there's evidence to the effect that foreigners had taken civilians out of Maline to a particular place. So my question to you would be: If in fact you are correct that the HVO was the army in control, would it --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps my learned colleague could be more specific because she has referred to evidence according to which foreigners took civilians out of Maline. I don't think it's necessary for me to suggest anything to the witness or confuse the witness. But we know what sort of evidence we have about civilians leaving Maline and about the people who took them or escorted them out of Maline. We have heard a lot about this. So I would be grateful if my learned colleague could rephrase the question in the light of the evidence that has been presented before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, could you reformulate, could you rephrase your question, please? The objective is the same, but rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'll try my best, Mr. President, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me if I say that the HVO army, were they the army that was in control, as you have alleged, on 8th June, 1993, in Maline? If, as you say, the HVO was the army, would it be possible then for foreigners to attack Croats in Maline or Gornje Maline or kidnap Croats in Gornje Maline at that time? Or do you think that in your opinion if the HVO was the army in control, that that would have been allowed?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't been understood correctly. When I refer to the 8th of June, I'm talking about the period of day during which the HVO had control in Gornje Maline. And the army had control in Donje Maline on the second part of the day, the second part of the day after the combat in the early morning hours which lasted for a few hours. So in the second part of the day, the BH army and its units established control over that area, lifted the blockade of Donje Maline, and set off with its forces in the direction of Guca Gora. In order to assist Krpeljici and Velika Bukovica that had also been encircled and were requesting assistance. So on the second part of -- in the second part of the 8th of June, the HVO didn't have control over the area that we have been referring to as Gornje Maline in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And Donje Maline did not suffer -- or rather, did Donje Maline suffer much damage in the combat? Would you say that Gornje Maline suffered more?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 7th or 8th of June? I'm not sure which date you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, we're talking --

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I apologise. There was fighting on the 7th of June when the HVO attacked the army positions in the village of Maline. And on the following day, on the 8th of June, combat operations were conducted in the area. So on both days, damage was inflicted on buildings in Donje Maline and in Gornje Maline. This could be seen in one of the documents that you produced. Naturally, there were various comments in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that precisely was my question to you. I wanted to find out at the end of the combat which village had the most destroyed houses, Donje Maline or Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I think more houses were destroyed in Gornje Maline in the course of the fighting during that two-day period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you agree with me I'm sure if I say to you that the Croatian civilians suffered more at the end of this combat?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Naturally after everything that had happened on that day, one must be frank and say that it wasn't easy. And at that time, their situation was worse than the situation the Bosniaks were in. But from that point in time, the Bosniaks were in a worse position than the Croats, as said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that is -- could you hold a second. Mr. President, that's the -- that concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's 25 past 12.00. We'll have our break now and we'll resume at about 10 to 1.00 for Defence counsel's re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel, you may proceed with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tarakcija, in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague you said that you were in a battalion and there was a brigade before you, in front of you and that meant they were more powerful than you were. When you mentioned this, tell me whether you were referring to the area of your battalion or were you referring to the entire Bila Valley area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I'll try and clarify this. In the area where the 2nd Mountain Battalion of the 306th Brigade was located, there was an HVO brigade, the Frankopan Brigade, which had its headquarters in Guca Gora. I could not say how many men this brigade singled out for the combat operations it was engaged in at the time in the inhabited places I mentioned. These places were totally blocked by its forces. I couldn't say how these HVO units were deployed. But I do know that all the inhabited places where the 2nd Mountain Battalion recruited its men, and this concerned six villages in which Bosniaks lived. I do know that these villages were almost totally encircled. As to how many men there were from that brigade surrounding those places I have mentioned, I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the facts that you had direct knowledge of and that related to your battalion, did you know who in April and May held the dominant positions, the elevations, throughout the Bila Valley. Who was at those positions?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that the HVO forces were at those positions. I could see that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that territory, was it possible to control the entire Bila Valley or only parts of it from those positions or was it possible to control the entire valley?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, I think that this made it possible to control about two-thirds of the Bila Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time in April and May, did you know whether in the Bila Valley territory in addition to the Frankopan Brigade forces, were there any other HVO forces present there, in addition to the Frankopan Brigade forces?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but I heard from others that in the Bila area or more specifically in the Guca Gora settlement, I heard that there were people who were not from the area in addition to the Frankopan Brigade forces. Some said that they saw some individuals who were not from the Guca Gora area and they were wearing the insignia of the Croatian army. This is not something I personally saw but this is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time in April and May 1993 the HVO had better equipment and better weapons for combat?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, when compared to us, when compared to what we could attain at the time, and given the embargo on providing weapons and given the possibility that the HVO, the HVO had to obtain help from neighbouring countries, we could see that they had better weapons and they could provide their units with sufficient equipment and they could replenish their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about your duty, the assistant commander for moral guidance and pursuant to that my learned friend put a number of questions to you. I'm asking you now whether the awareness of all your men that they were facing the enemy who was better equipped and in better position, was that an important factor for the morale and factor important for your efforts when you tried to explain the situation to your men?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Obviously our troops knew that the HVO was much better equipped and much better armed. However, regardless of the fact that we were in an inferior position, we did not have a way out. There was no way out. We had to motivate people. We had to defend our homes, our children, our families. I don't know whether this is a good answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this Chamber a military expert testified and provided his expert report. He said that several factors have an impact on the morale of units. Since you were engaged on those things, would you agree with this expert?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of factors which may play a role -- may play a negative or a positive role on -- in combat morale of units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've just asked you about two facts. The first fact was better equipment, and the second fact was the better position of the enemy. Since you've already answered this question, could you please confirm that these factors did have an impact on the morale of your men?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that some events in the Lasva Valley had an influence on the entire area. Tell me, did these events reflect on the morale of your fighters,? I'm primarily referring to the fact that the enemy had committed crimes in the valley involving civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it did have an impact on the overall situation in the unit and the feelings of every individual person when they heard what had happened in the neighbouring municipalities. This did have an impact on the combat morale and the readiness to perform combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, all of these elements that you have mentioned so far, to which extent did they have an impact on discipline and to which extent they required additional efforts from you to explain all that to your men and to maintain discipline in your units?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what was going on in the neighbouring municipalities and in the territory where we were, the checkpoints that we have mentioned, and bearing in mind what was going on at those checkpoints which were set up by the HVO and all the humiliation that members of our units suffered at the hands of the HVO and that their family members suffered, all this caused certain problems in our ranks and in our effort to reduce the tensions that existed, we had to invest a lot of effort, everyday conversations with group and individuals. We had to persuade them not to retaliate, not to behave in the way that would compound the situation. I had to do everything possible to change the situation for the better, to prevent the opening of a second front line since we already had one very busy front line facing the Serbians and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end I would like to ask you this: Since you have mentioned all of these factors that had an influence on the morale and all the measures that you took in order to help your soldiers behave in accordance with the rule of warfare, when you are looking at all these things from this perspective, when you look back at the year 1993 and the circumstances you faced at the time, did you do everything possible in order to discipline your soldiers, in order to prevent the BiH army members from committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the circumstances that we faced, I believe that an individual -- I did everything I could, everything that my physical and mental abilities enabled me to do to prevent members of my unit from doing anything that wouldn't be in accordance with the rules you have just mentioned. How successful I was I leave to the others to say. My superiors were aware of my personal engagement. My other colleagues, other officers also did everything possible. They invested a lot of effort in accordance with their means and abilities to prevent and avoid any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This will be my last question. My learned friend asked you whether your battalion and later on your brigade were parts of the 3rd Corps. From your point of view and from the position in which you were in the year 1993, could you tell us whether this position that you have just presented was also a requirement and an order that came to you from the 3rd Corps of the BiH army that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: There are a number of written and oral orders that came from our superior commands and our superior officers, starting with the 3rd Corps, the various brigades, battalions. And according to these orders, every member of the BiH army should behave in the way that I have just described. Those orders spoke to the effect that we should behave in the way that we should, unlike those that had carried out this aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions to put to you, but first I'm going to ask Mr. Registrar to provide the witness with a map which was admitted into evidence yesterday. I would like the witness to be shown this map. This is P137. Can you please put the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map of the region around Maline. Could you please take a marker and show us where you were on the day of the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in or zoom out. I can't see too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see Maline in the right-hand side corner. Where were you on the morning of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Gornje Maline on this map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can see that. Where were you, you yourself, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I was here, in this part of Donje Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be more precise. Where were you? In which part of Maline were you, Donje Maline that is? Don't write anything on the map, just show us.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The command post was here. I don't know whether the building itself is here, but the command post was around here. So there was a command post there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please show us where the command post was.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that it was in this part of Donje Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. If I understand you well, you have explained to us that Maline was encircled by the HVO. Could you please show us on this map how Maline was encircled by the HVO. Where were the HVO troops in the morning of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The HVO forces were here, in this area here above Gornje Maline. This was their defence line facing Mehurici. And then it descended to Postinje. They also had their forces deployed in this part where Gornje and Donje Maline are in contact. This is where they linked up and they had a line in the direction of Guca Gora. I apologise. Just give me a minute. So this is the line towards Guca Gora. I'm talking about their deployment that I was aware of at the time. Obviously from the direction of Guca Gora the HVO forces were here in front of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. On the 8th of June what time did you wake up? You were asleep and what time did you wake up on the morning of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Around 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you awake at 4.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Because I heard very loud shooting coming from all sides in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the shooting, was it mortar fire? Was it infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: It was mostly from infantry weapons, small arms, but there was also mortar shells being fired at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I'm asking you this because the mortar fire could be interesting. The mortar fire, where did this come from? Where did the mortar shells come from? And who was it who fired mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know who it was. In any case, fire came from both sides, from the HVO positions and also from the positions at which the combat took place above the village of Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you, understand that you had about 120 of your troops with you, members of your battalion. Now, did any of you see where this fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In this situation when we could hear shooting coming from the directions which we didn't control, the shooting came from the area above Gornje Maline towards the direction of Mehurici, Vranjaca and from the direction of Guca Gora. And since there was shooting opened on Donje Maline and Guca Gora, we ordered fire to be opened from our positions towards the positions of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the situation. It is 4.00 in the morning. There are mortar -- there's mortar fire. There's shooting from all over the place. Did you have any means of communication with your command post in Krpeljici? Did you inform them about this shooting? Did you know what was going on? Were you aware of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The -- our only communication was via a Motorola radio which didn't function too well between Maline and Krpeljici. But when we are in a position to convey information on the events in Maline, we did it via Bandol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you do it for the first time, at what time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: In the early morning hours we were not in a position to convey information on what was going on in Maline. We didn't communicate with the battalion command. It was only maybe one or two hours later that we managed to get in touch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At what time did you have your first contact with the other officers that belonged to your unit, at what time?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning. We managed to establish communication. I apologise, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it you yourself who used the Motorola in order to establish this contact?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Our communications man who was at the command post used a communication means in Bandol. Bear in mind that the configuration of the grounds was such that we could not communicate directly from Maline to Krpeljici, so the communications man conveyed a message via Bandol in -- and then the communications man in Bandol conveyed this message to the battalion commander. We did not have any direct communication with the battalion commander. At that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 6.00 you established contact. Did you receive any orders in return?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: At that moment we did not have any other orders. Our only order was to defend ourselves under the circumstances and to try and protect the settlement from the possible breakthrough of the HVO forces. At that moment Bandol came under a fierce HVO attack and we only learned that when once we established contact with the person who was in charge of those things in the village of Bandol. At that time we did not have any other orders. Our only order was to protect the village from the possible attack. I am not sure that at this moment the command in Krpeljici had the full picture of what was going on in Maline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, it is 6.00 in the morning, you have a radio contact. And according to what you've just said the HVO had encircled you. And during the course of this morning, how were -- how did the situation develop? How did you regain control of the area? What happened according to you? What allowed you to regain the control from the HVO that had encircled you up to then? Can you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said that we had established contact between 6.00 and 7.00, and I can't be sure of the exact time. At that moment the HVO forces which were deployed in the prominent elevations above both Donje and Gornje Maline, and I'm talking about their positions facing Mehurici and the forces which were deployed in the village itself and the forces that were deployed facing Guca Gora, those forces opened fire on ours. But we didn't know that the BiH army forces from the direction of Mehurici were advancing in their attempt to lift the blockade from Velika Bukovica and Krpeljici. The fighting between the army and the HVO was taking place in Vranjaca. This was the first shooting we heard and this shooting then moved across the whole line. We didn't know what was going on. We only knew that there was shooting opened on Maline and on our line. This shooting was opened -- this fire was opened by the HVO. Later on their lines on the prominent elevations above Maline that I've just pointed at on the map were taken by the BiH army, and the BiH army forces which were moving from the direction of Mehurici, primarily the 1st Battalion and the 4th Battalion, started advancing towards Krpeljici, Velika Bukovica, and Guca Gora. And then at one point in time, I don't know when, we received our task from the battalion commander. I suppose that at that time he had learned that forces of the 1st and 4th Battalions were moving in order to lift the blockade, and he asked from us in Maline to engage our forces in the attempt to take the positions in the direction of Guca Gora. Later on we managed to link up our forces with the troops from Krpeljici and the troops of the 3rd Mountain Brigade -- Battalion from the direction of Han Bila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forces, BiH forces, that came from Mehurici, how come there was only the 1st and the 4th Battalions of the 306th? Were there any other units, apart from those two battalions that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the troops of the 1st and the 4th Mountain Battalions of the 306th Brigade were given the task to lift the blockade from the settlements that we have mentioned. I don't know whether there were any other troops engaged in those combat operations. And I wouldn't be able to say anything about that because I was not engaged on that axis. The only thing I can talk about are the things that happened later on once we managed to take those lines. I don't know what happened before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you received your orders to start moving towards Guca Gora. You left your positions, your command post. At what time did you start advancing towards Guca Gora? When was that?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. I can't be sure of the time, but I believe that this was around 9.00 or 10.00, between 9.00 and 10.00. I personally was already on the line that we had taken earlier on; this was the line facing Guca Gora. And I asked from those who were in combat with me to start moving other troops from Maline towards Guca Gora because the combat was being transferred towards Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you well, at around 9.00 or 10.00 you started moving towards Guca Gora, which means that you must have had contacts with those what had arrived from Mehurici, the 1st and the 4th Battalion. Did you see them or did you not see them? You left for Guca Gora in a vehicle, as you have already told us. Did you see your fellow fighters who had arrived from Mehurici? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're talking about the 8th of June, if I'm not mistaken. I did not say that I took a vehicle on the 8th of June. I went on foot because the distance between Maline and Guca Gora is only 2 kilometres. So I went on foot and I moved towards Guca Gora, the defence line there, together with other men. At that time I did not have the possibility to see anybody from the 1st and 4th Battalions because their task was not to be active in that part where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, you didn't see them. In Maline, were there HVO troops and in those parts of Maline were inhabited by Croats, were there any HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: You mean generally speaking, yes. Able-bodied men from Gornje Maline were members from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you left Maline, did you see HVO soldiers anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I did not see any HVO soldiers in that situation when we were moving our troops, that is our unit -- when our unit was being moved towards Guca Gora. I didn't see any HVO soldiers at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just summarise what you've just told us. You have told us that at 4.00 in the morning on the 8th of June you were awoken by the sound of shooting. At that moment you were able to observe shooting coming from all directions. At around 6.00 you established contact with the communications man who was able to establish communication line. You sent a message that there was movement of troops from Mehurici to Maline. And then you received orders to leave for Guca Gora, and you left Maline around 9.00 on foot and you never saw the reinforcement coming to Maline. And you did not see any HVO soldiers in Maline. Is that what you've just told us? You didn't see anybody surrender in Maline.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't see any of them because I did not move along the axis where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After these developments, were you asked to submit a written report on what had happened on that day and the day before? Were you asked to submit a written report on the state of morale in light of the fact that there had been an attack? Were you asked to submit a report.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to submit such a report. I didn't submit such a report because this situation was a situation of intense combat and in such a situation it was not -- it would not have been possible to draft such a report, even if it had been asked, because it would have taken means and time for me to draft such a report and submit it to my command. Obviously our estimation of the situation was based on oral reports to the superior commands. I'm mainly talking about the 8th of June and the days surrounding that date up to maybe the 15th of June. During that period of time, we were not in a position to submit any written reports and send them to our superior command. The system of command and control over our unit was established only after the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 8th of June, you did not have any orders from your commanders regarding the possibility of an HVO offensive or a BiH army offensive? You did not have any written documents to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Given the blockades which were in place during that period in question, I was not in the position to see any written orders that would imply preparations for attacks or anything that an order of that sort would imply. Because the battalion command was also blocked, the brigade command was in three different localities, and we did not have any other means of communications, save for that Motorola that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have two more minor questions before I end. When you were in Maline, there were 120 men with you. As far as the HVO forces in Maline are concerned, how many of them were there? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I couldn't say because we didn't estimate their numbers, and naturally it wasn't possible for us to assess the strength of the HVO forces at their defence lines that I indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we have the Maline map before us. We can see that there are a series of houses there, and we have upper Maline and lower Maline. We have been talking about the 8th of June. On the 6th and 7th of June, could you walk around upper Maline where HVO soldiers were present? Was it possible to move around Maline before the 8th of June? Did you do so and did you go to upper Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No. The blockade had already been established. The lines had already been established by that date. And between the houses at the line of contact between the Bosniak and Croatian part, it wasn't possible to pass through those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they couldn't come to see you and you couldn't go to see them because there was a demarcation line, a line that separated you, and were there soldiers who were at the line around the clock, at these lines?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Naturally there were men at the defence lines all the time. That concerns our forces, and I assume the case was the same on the other side because this could be observed from the positions that we held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one last question. If I have understood you correctly. On the 4th of June they launched an attack. Did you sustain any casualties? Were there any wounded men? Because the HVO attack seems to have been a large-scale attack, so were any men in your battalion wounded on that morning between 4.00 and 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Mr. President, are we talking about the 7th or the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The 8th of June. On the 8th of June we had two lightly wounded soldiers. They had been wounded in the course of the combat operation on the 8th of June in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution want to ask any further questions? Ms. Henry-Benjamin, no questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I have just two questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In response to the question by the Bench you indicated there was shooting in Gornje Maline. But would you have observed if there was any looting and burning in the area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Naturally after the shooting broke out at the positions I have mentioned around Maline, some buildings caught fire as a result of the fighting. On the whole, I think the buildings concerned were in Gornje Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When I speak of dwellings, houses, would you have noticed if there were any houses on fire, burning, and if there might have been looting of these properties?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Do you mean on the 8th of June or at any other time?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the 8th of June and perhaps a little later after, on the night and the next morning?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June in the course of the fighting, some houses also caught fire. I don't know how many. You have a list in the document. This was a record compiled by the civilian protection. Some buildings which could catch fire easily were on fire. Naturally, after all those events in the following days there was looting, too. Looting occurred in parts of the settlement that had been abandoned by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And just one more question, sir. You indicated to the Bench that there were blockades set up by the HVO. But I'm not sure if you said earlier on in the testimony, and maybe you could clarify for us, did the ABiH have blockades set up as well?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Earlier on I said that in the army we tried to warn our members that they shouldn't retaliate in kind, that is to say they shouldn't set up blockades. On the whole, the HVO members had checkpoints at certain positions and later they blocked all inhabited places. As a result, we had to establish a defence line facing them so that we could defend our villages and its population.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So from your response, am I correct in assuming that the ABiH also had checkpoints in place? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I notice that the previous question, this question, has nothing to do with the questions that you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question as directly to what I asked the witness. The witness said in response to our question, to my question, said that the village was separated into parts, since there was the upper and the lower part. The HVO was in the upper part and they were in the lower part. And there was a line that had been established between the two parts. The Prosecution wants to know whether there were checkpoints at this line. The witness can answer the question. Witness, you have heard the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there weren't checkpoints there anymore. These defence lines had been fully established on both sides. I wasn't referring to checkpoints that one would have to pass through. There were defence lines and this meant that we had to mount a defence if an attack was launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there were no checkpoints, it was a defence line. This question has helped us clarify the matter. Ms. Henry-Benjamin, any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: None thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to clarify a few things, I'll just ask the witness several questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 7th of June when Donje Maline was attacked, who was in Donje Maline, the members of which army were there?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Members of the 2nd Mountain Battalion of the 306th Brigade were there. In Donje Maline there were also members of the 312th Mountain Brigade who were on leave with their families because their families had been expelled from Vlasic, Karaula, and from other parts of Travnik municipality. So the members of the 312th who were in Donje Maline on leave with their families and they were under the blockade that I have mentioned, they were there together with members of the 306th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the 120 men you have mentioned, what sort of the weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Infantry weapons. Not all of the men had the infantry weapons. They would take turns to use it. And they also had the weapons that the population had from before, for example, hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, who was in control of Gornje Maline on the 7th of June? Which army had full control over Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: The HVO forces had control there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is something you have already clarified in response to a question put to you by the Chamber. On the 7th of June a combat line had already been established between the villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, when the Presiding Judge put a question to you, you said that in the afternoon on the 8th of June you were heading in the direction of Guca Gora. Tell me, when did you yourself drive through Guca Gora? When was the first time you did this after the combat operations on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I think it was on the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, on the 8th, on the 9th, and on the 10th while you were in the area, did you at any time enter the area of Gornje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on in response to a question I put to you, you said that the first time you entered Gornje Maline was after 20 or 25 days. Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that later certain property was looted. Tell me, when you arrived there 20 or 25 days after the 8th of June, was that the first time you found out about the looting of property from abandoned houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to point out to the Defence that I asked no questions about looting. Please restrict your questions to the 8th of June. I didn't ask any questions about looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But my learned colleague did ask such a question, so I thought it would be good for the witness to clarify his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the question very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, when I was in Gornje Maline during that period I noticed that houses in which Croats had lived had been looted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question: Do you know who was involved in the looting and who controlled and protected the buildings at the time in your area?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: I didn't know who the perpetrators were, but I knew that the civilian police, the Ministry of the Interior, was responsible for controlling the area that had been left by the Croatian inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tarakcija, you said that the 1st and 4th Battalion of the 306th had to lift the blockade in the direction of Mehurici? They had to go from Mehurici towards Maline?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the 1st and 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade carried out that task?

utterances.speaker: SALIM TARAKCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank you for having come to testify here. We wish you a good trip home and I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope I have been of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes. Tomorrow we will be sitting at 9.00 and we have another witness scheduled for tomorrow. Thank you and I will see everyone here tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
